articleTitle: The definition of instrument performance for contract and metrological purposes
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: An instrument specification is intended to define its performance for any purpose where this is important. When an instrument is being chosen and purchased, the specification is one of the most significant features which decides to which company the contract will be awarded. When the instrument is put into service, the user will depend on the specification to satisfy himself that his measurements are of the required parameter and quality. The user may also have to convince an independent assessor of these. The author discusses the origin and purpose of specifications and discusses problems due to the ambiguity and lack of uniformly interpretable data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: With the advent of the industrial revolution, and mass production, bringing a wider choice of products to a wider market, the specification sheet evolved according to the manufacturers wish to influence the buyer in a specific direction that this product would meet their requirements. This paper highlights some aspects of the specification data sheet and suggests that customers should ask more questions from their suppliers. A more complete explanation can be found in a published document available from the author's company.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Instrument specifications-what do they really mean? Fibre optic instrumentation specifications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: Optical fibre measurements are becoming more demanding at all levels and is following that path which RF and microwave technology has covered many years ago, clarification and standardisation of specifications. It is essential for the optical instrumentation industry to fully support the future expansion and implementation of the 'all transparent optical network'.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The NAMAS approach to instrument specifications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: Instrument specifications provide an essential guide to users about the performance that can be expected from electrical test equipment and measurement standards. This paper examines some of the aspects of instrument specifications and identifies the important areas where specifications have to be proved (or otherwise) by traceable measurements with appropriate uncertainties. NAMAS requirements for traceability and calibration are stringent but not unreasonable when seen from a scientific viewpoint. In many cases the secondary characteristics of an instrument, such as input resistance or temperature coefficient, can be determined in a practical manner without too much difficulty. In other cases the manufacturer's specification can be used, where it appears reasonable, with verification of the performance of the equipment being established by internal comparisons or measurement audits.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: Instrumentation technology is changing apace. More and more devices are being produced which cover a plethora of functions with the consequent catalogue of specifications. This is good news for the customer since such devices usually represent very good value for money. However, the problems of choice are increased. It is in this area where good technical advice on the capabilities of an instrument are so important. So often devices are marketed through agents who necessarily do not have first-hand knowledge of all of the salient features of an instrument. From a customer viewpoint, it would be useful if instrument specifications contained a brief description of the working principles and also a contact address for technical information. In this way a customer may have a better chance of finding an instrument with a specification which truly meets his measurement needs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: A detailed description, including dimensions and other quantities, of the function, construction, materials, and quality of a manufactured article or an engineering project, is one definition of specifications presented. The details are important, and are sometimes where competitive advantage can be found. Often what is not stated is more important than what is stated. There are recognized and accepted meanings for the words and phrases used in oscilloscope specifications. IEEE Standard 1057 covers the term definitions used in Digitizing Oscilloscope specifications. These definitions describe and determine how the specifications apply to specific measurements. This article explains these definitions and shows how they apply to measurement applications. Specifications discussed include update rate, dynamic range, offset accuracy, gain accuracy, bandwidth, effective bits, and timing accuracy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: This paper discusses some examples of the relationship between circuit performance parameters and instrument specifications for signal measuring and sourcing instruments such as precision digital multimeters and calibrators.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Relating product specifications to measurements standards
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Instrument Specifications - What do they really mean?
abstract: The relating of product specifications to measurement standards must be undertaken with great care. It is very easy to overlook important sections of the product performance particularly in the so called 'grey' areas and at the borders and limits of the specification. Many users however seem to use the products in these 'grey' areas to make measurements sometimes oblivious of the risks they are taking. Unfortunately, there is no easy solution to the problem of relating product specifications to measurement standards. It is necessary to pay careful attention how the individual parts of the specification are used and combined to demonstrate the product performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
